concerns.text: The study curates 1 000 prompts but collects human feasibility scores for only 200 (100 conflicting, 100 neutral). All primary statistical tests (paired t‑test / Wilcoxon) are performed on this 200‑sample subset, which yields an estimated power of ≈0.70 (see Power Analysis section). This falls short of the commonly required ≥0.80 power for detecting a medium effect (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.5) and contradicts the project's own success criteria that assume sufficient power. The sample size is therefore insufficient to reliably support the causal claim that graph augmentation mitigates degradation.

Alignment is defined in the spec as the absolute difference between verifier output and human feasibility (lower is better), yet the plan computes an `alignment_delta = verifier_score - human_score` (which can be negative). Using raw difference instead of absolute difference changes the construct being measured and may bias the statistical comparison, violating construct validity.

The power analysis acknowledges limited power (≈0.70) but proceeds without a mitigation strategy (e.g., increasing the number of human‑annotated prompts or using a more sensitive statistical design). This leaves the primary hypothesis under‑powered, risking a false‑negative conclusion and undermining the causal inference.
